entries.expression: Unlike {comparison class}, which {defining behavior}, our approach {distinct behavior}.
entries.guidance: Keep the grammatical comparison parallel and verify that the characterization holds for the cited comparison class.
entries.meaning: Contrasts two methods on one explicit mechanism or assumption.

provenance.note: Original reusable pattern authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Do not use 'novel' as a substitute for explaining what is contributed.
examples: Our main contribution is {method or analysis} that {capability} under {evaluated conditions}.
entries.expression: Our main contribution is {artifact or insight} that {verified capability}.
entries.guidance: Name a method, analysis, dataset, benchmark, or finding. Bind the capability to the evaluated scope.
entries.meaning: States the central contribution and its demonstrated capability in one sentence.

provenance.note: Original reusable pattern authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Do not imply that a local convention is the field's only accepted definition.
examples: We use {term} to denote {entity or process satisfying explicit conditions}.
entries.guidance: Use when the paper needs a definition whose scope is specific to the present formulation. State the defining property, not a circular synonym.
entries.meaning: Introduces a local, operational meaning for a term.

provenance.note: Original reusable pattern authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Do not use this frame to silently redefine a standard term for rhetorical convenience.
examples: In this work, {term} refers specifically to {property within the studied setting}.
entries.expression: In this work, {term} refers to {scope-bounded definition}.
entries.guidance: Use when community usage is broader than the aspect studied in the paper. Follow with inclusions or exclusions if ambiguity remains.
entries.meaning: Defines a term while making the scope of the definition explicit.

provenance.note: Original reusable pattern authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Do not call a comparison controlled when data, compute, architecture, or tuning differs materially.
examples: For a controlled comparison, we hold {data and compute budget} fixed and vary only {model component}.
entries.expression: For a controlled comparison, we hold {factor} fixed and vary only {factor}.
entries.guidance: Use only when the protocol truly controls the named factor; list remaining mismatches if they affect interpretation.
entries.meaning: Explains how an experiment isolates a comparison dimension.

provenance.note: Original reusable pattern authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Do not erase the contribution of the foundational method.
examples: Our formulation builds on {named framework} and extends it to {setting} by {technical modification}.
entries.expression: Our formulation builds on {foundation} and extends it to {new setting or capability}.
entries.guidance: Cite the foundation and explain what changes in the new formulation. Use 'extends' only when the technical relationship is real.
entries.meaning: States intellectual continuity and the precise extension contributed by the paper.

provenance.note: Original reusable pattern authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Do not write as though the proposed future experiment has already succeeded.
examples: An important next step is to evaluate {capability} under {distribution shift or deployment condition}.
entries.expression: An important next step is to evaluate {capability} under {condition}.
entries.guidance: Use for work not completed in the current paper. Prefer a falsifiable next step over generic aspirations.
entries.meaning: Identifies a concrete unresolved evaluation or research direction.

provenance.note: Original reusable pattern authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Do not claim that all existing methods fail when only a subset was examined.
examples: Despite progress in {capability}, existing methods remain limited by {assumption or failure mode} in {setting}.
entries.expression: Despite progress in {area}, existing methods remain limited by {specific limitation}.
entries.guidance: The limitation must be supported and relevant to the proposed contribution. Specify the affected regime, assumption, or metric.
entries.meaning: Identifies a research gap without dismissing prior progress.

provenance.note: Original reusable pattern authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Do not turn a limitation into an unsupported claim that future work will certainly solve it.
examples: Our evaluation is limited to {tasks or environments}; robustness to {shift} remains to be established.
entries.expression: Our evaluation is limited to {scope}; performance under {unseen condition} remains to be established.
entries.guidance: Name the missing population, environment, scale, horizon, embodiment, or distribution. Do not bury a material limitation.
entries.meaning: States an evaluation boundary and separates tested from untested conditions.

provenance.note: Original reusable pattern authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Avoid an empty claim such as 'This is a very challenging problem.'
examples: A central challenge is to {achieve capability} while {respecting data, compute, safety, or deployment constraint}.
entries.expression: A central challenge is to {objective} while {constraint}.
entries.guidance: Name both the desired capability and the condition that makes it difficult. Prefer measurable constraints over adjectives such as challenging or complex.
entries.meaning: Motivates a problem through a concrete objective–constraint tension.

provenance.note: Original reusable pattern authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Do not invent a taxonomy whose categories overlap without explanation.
examples: Prior approaches differ primarily in how they {technical axis one} and whether they {technical axis two}.
entries.expression: Prior approaches differ primarily in {axis one} and {axis two}.
entries.guidance: Choose axes that expose meaningful assumptions or design choices, then place representative methods along them with citations.
entries.meaning: Organizes related work by technical comparison axes instead of paper-by-paper chronology.

provenance.note: Original reusable pattern authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Avoid claiming complete novelty merely because the exact combination has not appeared.
examples: Our setting is most closely related to {method family}, but differs in its assumption of {assumption} and its objective of {objective}.
entries.expression: Our setting is most closely related to {family}, but differs in {assumption or objective}.
entries.guidance: Name the closest family before the distinction. The difference should be technically consequential, not cosmetic.
entries.meaning: Positions the present work relative to the nearest literature family.

provenance.note: Original reusable pattern authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Avoid 'significant' unless statistical significance was actually tested.
examples: {method} improves mean {metric} by {absolute or relative value} over {baseline} under the {protocol} protocol.
entries.guidance: State whether the value is absolute or relative, and match the aggregation and uncertainty used in the table.
entries.meaning: Reports a quantified comparison with its baseline and protocol.

provenance.note: Original reusable pattern authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Do not say 'we agree' and then dismiss the concern without engaging it.
examples: We agree that {evaluation dimension} is important; our current evidence addresses {specific subset}, while {uncovered condition} remains outside scope.
entries.expression: We agree that {concern} is important; our current evidence addresses {covered scope}.
entries.guidance: Use when the concern is valid but broader than the submitted evidence. State the uncovered portion explicitly if space permits.
entries.meaning: Acknowledges a valid concern while delimiting what the current paper can support.

provenance.note: Original reusable pattern authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Do not begin with a long thank-you paragraph that delays the answer.
examples: Yes. {claim bounded to the question}; the supporting evidence is reported in {table, figure, section, or verified result}.
entries.expression: Yes. {direct answer}; the supporting evidence is {evidence pointer}.
entries.guidance: Use when the answer is genuinely yes. Replace the first token with 'No' or a qualified answer when appropriate; never force agreement.
entries.meaning: Answers a reviewer question immediately and then points to evidence.

provenance.note: Original reusable pattern authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Do not blame the reviewer for a misunderstanding caused by unclear writing.
examples: We apologize for the ambiguity: {term or claim} refers to {precise scope}, not {plausible alternative reading}.
entries.expression: We apologize for the ambiguity: {precise clarification}.
entries.guidance: Use only when the manuscript wording could reasonably cause the misunderstanding. Follow with the exact revision.
entries.meaning: Acknowledges unclear presentation and states the intended meaning directly.

provenance.note: Original reusable pattern authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Do not minimize a limitation that invalidates the main claim.
examples: This is a limitation of the current study, but it does not affect our conclusion about {claim within tested scope} because {reason}.
entries.expression: This is a limitation of the current study, but it does not affect {narrower conclusion}.
entries.guidance: Use only when the narrower conclusion truly survives the limitation. Explain why with evidence or logic.
entries.meaning: Makes a bounded concession while preserving a conclusion supported by existing evidence.

provenance.note: Original reusable pattern authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Do not use a cosmetic correction frame when the issue invalidates the main analysis.
examples: The reviewer is correct that {quantity or label} was stated incorrectly; we will replace it with {correct value} in {location}.
The reviewer is correct that our wording implied {overbroad claim}; we will narrow it to {supported scope}.
entries.expression: The reviewer is correct that {specific statement}; we will correct {location} accordingly.
entries.guidance: Name the exact error, give the corrected statement, and reassess any downstream conclusion that depends on it.
entries.meaning: Accepts a concrete factual or presentation error without conceding claims that are unaffected by it.

provenance.note: Original rebuttal pattern authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Do not invent a table location or imply that an indirect analysis answers the request.
examples: The requested comparison is already included in {Table or Appendix}, where {method} achieves {verified metric} under {protocol}.
entries.expression: The requested comparison is already included in {location}, where {verified result}.
entries.guidance: Give an exact manuscript location and reproduce numbers faithfully. If absent, use a revision or limitation frame instead.
entries.meaning: Points a reviewer to existing evidence and summarizes only the relevant result.

provenance.note: Original reusable pattern authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Do not call a comparison budget-matched when only one of several dominant resources is controlled.
examples: At a matched interaction budget of {value}, {method} obtains {metric}, compared with {baseline result}.
When parameter count is matched, the difference in {metric} is {value}.
entries.guidance: Name the matched resource and disclose other material differences. Report the exact statistic and uncertainty used in the manuscript.
entries.meaning: Frames a comparison under an explicitly controlled data, interaction, parameter, compute, or tuning budget.

provenance.note: Original reusable comparison pattern authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Do not imply that an unrun experiment produced a favorable result or promise a result whose outcome is unknown.
examples: We do not currently have evidence for robustness under {shift}; we will restrict the manuscript to the evaluated {scope}.
The requested comparison is not available in the current submission, so we will remove the corresponding general claim.
entries.expression: We do not currently have evidence for {broader claim}; we will restrict the manuscript to {supported claim}.
entries.guidance: Use when the requested experiment was not run or the available analysis is insufficient. Explain what existing evidence still supports.
entries.meaning: Responds to a request that cannot be supported with existing results by narrowing the claim instead of inventing evidence.

provenance.note: Original rebuttal pattern authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Avoid vague promises such as 'we will improve the paper.'
examples: We will revise {Section or caption} to make {assumption, protocol, or limitation} explicit.
entries.expression: We will revise {location} to make {point} explicit.
entries.guidance: Name the section, statement, figure, caption, or experimental detail and the information to add. Do not promise a new result unless it exists.
entries.meaning: Commits to a concrete presentation change in response to feedback.

provenance.note: Original reusable pattern authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Do not label directly competing methods as merely complementary to evade comparison.
examples: A complementary line of work studies {adjacent problem}, sharing our interest in {common element} but targeting {different objective}.
entries.expression: A complementary line of work studies {adjacent problem}.
entries.guidance: Explain the relationship after the topic sentence: shared tool, assumption, representation, or evaluation setting.
entries.meaning: Introduces adjacent literature that informs but does not directly solve the same problem.

provenance.note: Original reusable pattern authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Do not force heterogeneous work into one family merely because papers use similar architectures.
examples: These approaches share the objective of {objective}, but differ in their assumptions about {axis one} and {axis two}.
While both families address {problem}, they obtain supervision from {different sources}.
entries.expression: These approaches share {common objective}, but differ in {technical axes}.
entries.guidance: Support the shared property and each difference with verified citations. Select axes that connect directly to the present method.
entries.meaning: Synthesizes a family of papers through one commonality and one or more technically relevant differences.

provenance.note: Original reusable pattern authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Avoid a global default statement when several experiments use materially different protocols.
examples: Unless otherwise specified, we report the mean over {number} seeds and use {aggregation rule}.
Unless otherwise specified, all methods use the same {data, compute, or interaction budget}.
entries.expression: Unless otherwise specified, we use {default configuration} in all experiments.
entries.guidance: State the actual default and enumerate consequential exceptions where they occur. Do not use the frame to hide benchmark-specific tuning.
entries.meaning: Declares a shared experimental default while allowing explicitly identified exceptions.

provenance.note: Original reusable pattern authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Do not generalize beyond the evaluated settings or omit exceptions.
examples: Across {tasks or datasets}, {method} consistently improves {metric} over {named comparison set}.
entries.guidance: Use 'consistently' only when the pattern holds across the stated units. Name seeds, tasks, datasets, or metrics as appropriate.
entries.meaning: Reports a recurring empirical pattern with an explicit evaluation boundary.

provenance.note: Original reusable pattern authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Avoid a transition that merely repeats the distinction.
examples: This distinction matters because it determines whether {downstream consequence}.
entries.guidance: Use after defining two concepts or settings. The consequence should be explicit and locally relevant.
entries.meaning: Connects a technical distinction to its consequence for the argument or evaluation.

provenance.note: Original reusable pattern authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Do not upgrade a qualified Chinese claim into an unconditional English conclusion.
examples: Although {method} improves {metric} on {subset}, the difference is not statistically significant across {units}.
entries.guidance: Keep negation, modality, comparison direction, quantities, and citations attached to the same propositions as in the source.
entries.meaning: Preserves a concession and its qualification during Chinese-to-English reconstruction.

provenance.note: Original reusable pattern authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Avoid 'the experiments prove the effectiveness and superiority of our method.'
examples: Across {tasks}, {method} improves {metric} over {baselines} under a matched {budget}.
The ablation supports the contribution of {component} to {measured outcome} in {setting}.
entries.expression: replace vague effectiveness claims with the observed outcome
entries.guidance: Write the measured change directly. Use 'supports the effectiveness of' only when several results jointly justify the scoped judgment; use 'proves' only for a formal result.
entries.meaning: An effectiveness claim is informative only when it names the intervention, comparison, metric, and evaluated setting.

provenance.note: Original usage guidance authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Do not infer broad out-of-distribution generalization from a random train–test split over nearly identical samples.
examples: We evaluate generalization to unseen {objects or tasks} by holding out {unit} during training.
The current study does not establish transfer across unseen {embodiments or environments}.
entries.expression: name the generalization axis and held-out unit
entries.guidance: State what was held out during training and what unit is averaged at evaluation. Prefer 'generalization to unseen objects' over an unqualified 'generalization ability.'
entries.meaning: Generalization is always relative to a specified shift, such as unseen objects, tasks, environments, users, embodiments, or combinations.

provenance.note: Original cross-domain usage guidance authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Do not translate 可能 or 表明 into an unqualified 'proves', or assume that any two evidential verbs have a context-free ordering.
examples: The results suggest that {hypothesis}, but do not establish {stronger causal claim}.
entries.expression: Distinguish possibility, interpretation, empirical evidence, and formal proof.
entries.guidance: Use 'may/might' for possibility, 'suggests/supports' for a tentative interpretation or evidence relation, 'shows/demonstrates' for a result established within the study design, and 'proves' only for a formal proof under stated assumptions.
entries.meaning: Modal verbs and evidential verbs serve different functions rather than forming one universal strength ordering.

provenance.note: Original usage guidance authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Avoid mechanically translating 性能 into 'performances' or writing 'achieve better performances' without a metric.
examples: {method} improves performance on {benchmark}, as measured by {metric}.
The methods exhibit different performance profiles across {task groups}.
entries.expression: performance is usually a mass noun when reporting an aggregate result
entries.guidance: Prefer 'improves performance,' 'achieves higher task success,' or the exact metric. Use a plural only when the sentence explicitly distinguishes multiple kinds of performance.
entries.meaning: In empirical writing, 'performance' usually denotes aggregate measured behavior, whereas plural 'performances' is reserved for genuinely distinct acts or types of performance.

provenance.note: Original usage guidance authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Avoid using 'respectively' when one item maps to several values or when the antecedent order is unclear.
examples: The {first method} and {second method} obtain {first value} and {second value}, respectively.
We use {value one} for {setting one} and {value two} for {setting two}.
entries.expression: respectively requires an unambiguous one-to-one ordering
entries.guidance: Place 'respectively' close to the second list. If the mapping could be misread, split the sentence or state each pairing explicitly.
entries.meaning: Respectively maps two or more ordered lists element by element and should be used only when both lists have matching cardinality and a clear order.

provenance.note: Original usage guidance authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Do not infer statistical significance from a visibly larger mean, non-overlapping point estimates, or the Chinese adjective 显著 alone.
examples: {method} yields a {value}-point improvement, but the difference is not statistically significant under {test}.
The improvement is substantial relative to {reference scale}, with an effect size of {value}.
entries.guidance: Translate 显著 according to evidence: use 'statistically significant' only when a specified statistical analysis supports it; otherwise report the effect size or use a magnitude term justified by context.
entries.meaning: Statistical significance refers to an inferential test or interval criterion, whereas substantial, marked, or large describes effect magnitude and requires a stated scale.

provenance.note: Original usage guidance authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Never use 'state-of-the-art' as a general adjective for the method or as a synonym for strong.
examples: Under the {protocol} protocol, {method} achieves the best reported {metric} among {comparison set}.
entries.guidance: Use only after checking the benchmark, metric, split, protocol, contemporaneous comparison set, and direction of improvement. Prefer the exact result when the scope is narrow.
entries.meaning: A scoped claim that a verified result is best within a defined comparison set.

provenance.note: Original usage guidance authored for this repository.

entries.avoid: Do not call every two-network method actor–critic; the functional roles matter.
examples: The actor parameterizes {policy}, while the critic estimates {value quantity} for policy improvement.
We train the actor and critic from {real or imagined transitions}.
entries.guidance: State which value quantity the critic estimates, how the actor uses it, and whether updates are on-policy, off-policy, stochastic, or deterministic.
entries.meaning: A reinforcement-learning method with an actor that represents or updates the policy and a critic that estimates a value-related signal used to guide the actor.

provenance.note: Independent synthesis of linked primary sources; no source sentence copied.

entries.avoid: Do not interpret a positive estimated advantage as a universal guarantee that the action is optimal.
examples: We estimate $A^\pi(s,a)=Q^\pi(s,a)-V^\pi(s)$ and use it to weight the policy update.
Positive estimated advantages increase the relative likelihood of the sampled actions.
entries.guidance: Specify the policy and estimator. When using generalized advantage estimation or another approximation, name its bias–variance parameters.
entries.meaning: The difference between the action value and the state value under a policy, measuring how an action compares with the policy's average action at that state.

provenance.note: Independent definition based on standard policy-optimization formulations.

entries.avoid: Do not claim that every pessimistic penalty provides a valid lower bound.
examples: The objective regularizes Q-values for out-of-distribution actions while fitting Bellman targets on dataset transitions.
Conservative value estimation mitigates {specified offline optimization failure}.
entries.guidance: Describe the exact regularizer and theoretical or empirical property established by the cited method; conservative bias can trade off underestimation and robustness.
entries.meaning: Learning value estimates with an objective that penalizes overly high Q-values, especially for actions not supported by the offline dataset.

provenance.note: Independent synthesis of linked primary sources; no source sentence copied.

entries.avoid: Do not equate a global team reward with solved credit assignment.
examples: A counterfactual baseline improves credit assignment by comparing an agent's chosen action with {alternative actions} while holding {other agents} fixed.
The shared reward provides weak agent-specific credit in {setting}.
entries.guidance: State whether credit is temporal, agent-specific, or both. Explain the baseline or decomposition used to isolate an agent's contribution.
entries.meaning: The problem of determining how individual agents' actions contribute to a shared outcome so that each policy receives an informative learning signal.

provenance.note: Independent synthesis of linked primary sources; no source sentence copied.

entries.avoid: Do not equate a return distribution with epistemic uncertainty about the value estimate.
examples: The critic approximates the distribution of discounted returns with {atoms or quantiles}.
Actions are selected by the expectation of the learned return distribution.
entries.guidance: Specify the distributional parameterization, projection or regression objective, and how action selection reduces the distribution to a decision criterion.
entries.meaning: A value-based perspective that models a probability distribution over random returns rather than only their expected value.

provenance.note: Independent definition synthesized from the distributional RL formulation and its use in Rainbow.

entries.avoid: Do not assume replayed data are on-policy or independent and identically distributed.
examples: Transitions are stored in a replay buffer of capacity {size} and sampled uniformly for critic updates.
We sample length-{k} sequences from replay to train the recurrent world model.
entries.guidance: Report capacity, sampling distribution, sequence length, prioritization, and the ratio of updates to newly collected data when these affect results.
entries.meaning: A mechanism that stores previously collected transitions or trajectories and resamples them for subsequent learning updates.

provenance.note: Independent definition synthesized from off-policy deep RL and robotic learning methods.

entries.avoid: Do not describe entropy regularization as random action noise; it is part of the policy objective.
examples: We optimize a maximum-entropy objective that combines expected return with {temperature}-weighted policy entropy.
The temperature controls the reward–entropy trade-off.
entries.guidance: Define the sign, temperature, and whether the target entropy or temperature is learned. Avoid vague claims that entropy always improves exploration.
entries.meaning: A reinforcement-learning formulation that augments expected reward with a policy-entropy term, trading off task return and stochasticity according to a temperature parameter.

provenance.note: Independent synthesis of linked primary sources; no source sentence copied.

entries.avoid: Do not assert the Markov property for raw observations when the agent only has partial information.
examples: We model the task as an MDP {tuple}, where {symbol definitions}.
Because observations are partial, the policy conditions on {history or belief representation}.
entries.guidance: List the tuple used in the paper and define any departure, such as partial observability, finite horizon, goal conditioning, or multiple agents.
entries.meaning: A formal sequential decision process defined by states, actions, transition dynamics, and rewards, together with a discount factor or finite horizon when required by the formulation; the next-state distribution depends on the current state and action.

provenance.note: Independent synthesis of linked primary sources; no source sentence copied.

entries.avoid: Do not use 'distribution shift' without naming the two distributions being compared.
examples: Offline policy optimization can induce distribution shift by assigning probability to actions poorly covered by the dataset.
We regularize {policy or value estimate} toward the support of the behavior data.
entries.guidance: Specify whether the shift concerns states, actions, transitions, tasks, or observations. Connect the failure mode to bootstrapping or policy optimization when applicable.
entries.meaning: A mismatch between state–action distributions represented in a fixed dataset and those induced by the learned policy, which makes value estimates for unsupported actions unreliable.

provenance.note: Independent synthesis of linked primary sources; no source sentence copied.

entries.avoid: Do not call training from a continually growing replay buffer offline RL.
examples: We consider the offline RL setting, where the agent learns from a fixed dataset {D} and cannot collect additional transitions.
The dataset contains trajectories generated by {behavior policy mixture}.
entries.guidance: Describe dataset coverage, behavior policies if known, reward availability, and evaluation protocol. Distinguish offline RL from off-policy online learning and imitation learning.
entries.meaning: Reinforcement learning from a fixed dataset of previously collected transitions, without additional environment interaction during training.

provenance.note: Independent synthesis of linked primary sources; no source sentence copied.

entries.avoid: Do not describe supervised imitation from a fixed dataset as reinforcement learning unless a reward-based objective or RL update is used.
examples: We formulate {task} as reinforcement learning, where the agent observes {observation}, selects {action}, and receives {reward}.
The objective is to maximize the expected discounted return under {environment distribution}.
entries.guidance: Specify observation/state, action, reward, horizon or discount, and whether training is online or offline when these choices matter.
entries.meaning: A decision-making framework in which an agent interacts with an environment and learns behavior to maximize expected cumulative reward.

provenance.note: Independent synthesis of linked primary sources; no source sentence copied.

entries.avoid: Do not describe a return-conditioned model as optimizing return through online RL unless it actually performs such updates.
examples: The policy predicts the next action conditioned on {return-to-go} and {trajectory context}.
At inference, we condition the sequence model on {target return}.
entries.guidance: Specify tokenization, context, conditioning signal, and how desired returns are chosen at inference. Do not assume conditioning guarantees achievement of the requested return.
entries.meaning: Modeling actions as a sequence prediction problem conditioned on a desired return together with past states and actions.

provenance.note: Independent synthesis of linked primary sources; no source sentence copied.

entries.avoid: Do not use reward and return interchangeably: reward is typically per transition, whereas return aggregates rewards over time.
examples: The objective maximizes the expected discounted return {equation}.
We report undiscounted episode return while using {discount} for training.
entries.guidance: Define horizon, discount convention, termination handling, and whether reported return is undiscounted even if training uses discounting.
entries.meaning: The cumulative sum of future rewards, commonly weighting a reward received k steps later by a discount factor raised to k.

provenance.note: Independent synthesis of linked primary sources; no source sentence copied.

entries.avoid: Do not describe every loss across adjacent time steps as temporal-difference learning.
examples: We minimize a temporal-difference error against $r_t+\gamma V_{\bar\theta}(s_{t+1})$.
The latent value is trained with an $n$-step TD target.
entries.guidance: State the exact target, discount, update horizon, target network or stop-gradient treatment, and whether the estimate is on-policy or off-policy.
entries.meaning: Learning a value-related prediction by moving it toward a target that combines an observed reward with a bootstrapped estimate of subsequent value.

provenance.note: Independent definition synthesized from value-learning and TD-MPC formulations.

entries.avoid: Do not describe Q(s,a) as immediate reward or as a transition probability.
examples: The critic estimates the action-value function {Q symbol} under the current policy.
The state-value function provides {bootstrap or baseline role}.
entries.guidance: Define the policy and return convention under which the expectation is taken. Use Q-function as the standard short form for an action-value function.
entries.meaning: A state-value function estimates expected future return from a state under a policy, whereas an action-value function additionally conditions on the current action.

provenance.note: Independent synthesis of linked primary sources; no source sentence copied.

entries.avoid: Do not compare results taken from incompatible protocols without a caveat.
examples: We compare methods at matched environment-interaction budgets and report performance over {number} seeds using {aggregation}.
Because {prior result} uses a different data budget, we report it separately rather than treating it as a controlled baseline.
entries.expression: RL methods should be compared at matched interaction, data, and evaluation budgets.
entries.guidance: Report environment steps, dataset size, number of seeds, evaluation episodes, compute where relevant, and tuning access. Separate final performance from sample efficiency.
entries.meaning: Frames a fair reinforcement-learning comparison around the budgets that determine efficiency and performance.

provenance.note: Independent synthesis of linked primary sources; example wording is original.

entries.avoid: Do not describe it as ordinary behavior cloning when weights materially change the data contribution.
examples: The policy is trained by advantage-weighted behavioral cloning over actions in the offline dataset.
Weights are computed from {advantage estimate} with temperature {beta}.
entries.guidance: State the weighting function, temperature or clipping, and the source of advantage estimates. It remains constrained to observed actions at training time.
entries.meaning: A policy-learning objective that imitates dataset actions with weights increasing with an estimated advantage, favoring actions judged better than the state-dependent baseline.

provenance.note: Canonical term indexed from linked primary papers; examples are original.

entries.avoid: Do not use behavior policy as a synonym for learned target policy.
examples: The offline dataset was collected by an unknown mixture of behavior policies.
The target policy may select actions outside the support of the behavior data.
entries.guidance: Use when data provenance matters. If the dataset combines multiple or unknown collectors, state that rather than implying a single known policy.
entries.meaning: The policy or mixture of policies that generated the data used for learning, which may differ from the policy being evaluated or optimized.

provenance.note: Canonical term indexed from linked primary papers; examples are original.

entries.avoid: Do not imply that a bootstrapped target is unbiased or independent of the network being trained.
examples: The critic is updated toward a bootstrapped target computed with the target value network.
We stop gradients through the $n$-step return target.
entries.guidance: Name the prediction being reused and where gradients are stopped. Distinguish RL bootstrapping from statistical bootstrap resampling.
entries.meaning: A learning target that contains a prediction produced by the current model or a target model for a later state, rather than relying entirely on observed outcomes.

provenance.note: Field-standard RL terminology indexed from value-based and actor–critic methods.

entries.avoid: Do not call execution decentralized if agents require unavailable global information at test time.
examples: We adopt CTDE: the centralized critic conditions on {joint information}, whereas each actor observes only {local information}.
At execution time, agents act without {training-only signal}.
entries.guidance: Specify what is centralized—critic, value, state, communication, or data—and what each deployed policy observes.
entries.meaning: A multi-agent learning paradigm that permits access to joint or global information during training while each agent acts from locally available information at execution time.

provenance.note: Canonical term indexed from linked primary papers; examples are original.

entries.avoid: Do not claim that entropy regularization necessarily improves exploration or robustness in every environment.
examples: The actor maximizes expected return and policy entropy with temperature $\alpha$.
We adapt the entropy temperature toward a target entropy of {value}.
entries.guidance: State the entropy convention, coefficient or temperature, and whether it is fixed or adapted. Distinguish action entropy from state-distribution diversity.
entries.meaning: An objective term that rewards policy entropy in addition to task return, encouraging stochasticity according to a specified temperature or coefficient.

provenance.note: Field-standard terminology indexed from maximum-entropy actor–critic methods.

entries.avoid: Do not claim that an upper expectile is the maximum unless limiting conditions are established.
examples: The value function is fitted by expectile regression to emphasize high-valued actions present in the dataset.
We set the expectile parameter to {tau}.
entries.guidance: Define the expectile parameter and targets. Do not describe expectiles as quantiles; they use asymmetric squared rather than absolute loss.
entries.meaning: An asymmetric squared-loss regression objective whose expectile parameter emphasizes different portions of the target distribution; in IQL it is used to fit an upper expectile of in-dataset action values.

provenance.note: Canonical term indexed from linked primary papers; examples are original.

entries.avoid: Do not describe a dataset as diverse or well-covered solely because it contains many transitions.
examples: Performance degrades when the learned policy selects actions poorly represented in the offline dataset.
We report coverage across {tasks, states, actions, or embodiments} in addition to trajectory count.
entries.expression: state–action coverage of the offline dataset
entries.guidance: Operationalize coverage with dataset statistics, support assumptions, distances, or task-specific diagnostics; it is not captured by dataset size alone.
entries.meaning: The range and frequency of states and actions represented by a fixed dataset relative to those needed by a candidate policy or evaluation task.

provenance.note: Field-standard support and coverage concept synthesized across offline RL and multi-robot datasets.

entries.avoid: Do not call an arbitrary gradient through a policy network a policy-gradient estimator when it optimizes a supervised or model-predictive loss.
examples: We form the policy-gradient estimator with generalized advantage estimates from on-policy trajectories.
Importance weights correct the estimator for the difference between {behavior policy} and {target policy}.
entries.guidance: State the objective, sampling policy, advantage or return estimator, importance weights, and variance-reduction method.
entries.meaning: A sample-based estimate of the gradient of an expected-return objective with respect to policy parameters.

provenance.note: Field-standard terminology indexed from trust-region and actor–critic policy optimization.

entries.avoid: Do not call a value function or open-loop action sequence a policy.
examples: The stochastic policy {symbol} maps {observation or state} to a distribution over {actions}.
We condition the policy on {goal specification} in addition to {observation}.
entries.guidance: Use π(a|s) for a stochastic policy and state whether conditioning is on state, observation, goal, language, or history.
entries.meaning: A rule or conditional distribution that maps an agent's information state, such as an observation or history, to actions.

provenance.note: Canonical term indexed from linked primary papers; examples are original.

entries.avoid: Do not call a collection of value-network predictions a return distribution unless the learning formulation models random returns.
examples: We approximate the state–action return distribution $Z^\pi(s,a)$ with {representation}.
The expected value is recovered by taking the mean of the learned return distribution.
entries.guidance: Condition the distribution explicitly and distinguish its expectation from the full random-return law.
entries.meaning: The probability distribution of cumulative discounted reward induced by environment randomness and policy actions from a specified state or state–action pair.

provenance.note: Canonical distributional RL terminology indexed from the primary ICML paper.

entries.avoid: Do not infer sample efficiency from wall-clock speed or final performance alone.
examples: We evaluate sample efficiency by comparing {metric} after {matched number} environment steps.
The method reaches {performance threshold} using {data amount}.
entries.guidance: Name the sample unit—steps, episodes, demonstrations, images, or hours—and compare learning curves or performance at matched data budgets.
entries.meaning: The amount of environment interaction or training data required to reach a specified level of performance.

provenance.note: Canonical term indexed from linked primary papers; examples are original.

entries.avoid: Do not claim monotonic improvement for a practical approximation unless its assumptions and guarantee apply.
examples: The policy update is restricted by a KL-divergence constraint between {old and new policies}.
A trust region limits the step size in policy space.
entries.guidance: Specify whether the constraint is hard, approximate, or implemented through a penalty or clipped surrogate. Do not transfer theoretical guarantees across variants.
entries.meaning: A policy update constrained to keep the new policy sufficiently close to the old policy, commonly measured by KL divergence, to improve optimization stability.

provenance.note: Canonical term indexed from linked primary papers; examples are original.

entries.avoid: Do not infer overestimation solely because a policy performs poorly.
examples: The critic overestimates values for actions outside the dataset support.
We measure value overestimation by comparing {predicted quantity} with {reference return}.
entries.guidance: Identify the estimator and distribution on which overestimation is measured. In offline RL, relate it to actions not well supported by data when justified.
entries.meaning: Systematic upward bias in estimated values, often amplified when optimization selects actions whose estimates are erroneously high.

provenance.note: Canonical term indexed from linked primary papers; examples are original.

entries.avoid: Do not equate off-policy with offline: off-policy training may still collect new environment data.
examples: The algorithm is off-policy and reuses transitions from {replay buffer or fixed dataset}.
Unlike on-policy updates, the critic can learn from data collected by {behavior policy}.
entries.guidance: Describe the actual behavior and target policies, correction mechanism, and data reuse. Finite policy lag is an implementation approximation whose effect depends on the algorithm; recency alone does not make data on-policy.
entries.meaning: On-policy updates estimate or optimize the target policy using data generated by that same policy, whereas off-policy methods can learn about a target policy from data generated by a different behavior policy.

provenance.note: Independent synthesis of linked primary sources; no source sentence copied.

entries.avoid: Do not transfer a convergence or contraction statement from policy evaluation to control without checking the additional assumptions.
examples: The distributional operator is analyzed separately for fixed-policy evaluation and control.
Our theorem concerns policy evaluation; the control variant is assessed empirically.
entries.guidance: State whether a theoretical property or operator applies only under a fixed policy or also under policy improvement and maximization.
entries.meaning: Policy evaluation estimates returns for a fixed policy, whereas control additionally seeks or improves a policy to obtain higher return.

provenance.note: Independent scope distinction synthesized from RL theory and policy-optimization papers.

entries.avoid: Do not call a random trajectory split out-of-distribution evaluation without demonstrating a meaningful shift.
examples: The test tasks use held-out trajectories but remain within the dataset's object and action coverage.
Generalization beyond the behavior-policy support remains to be established.
entries.expression: distinguish interpolation within dataset support from extrapolation beyond it
entries.guidance: Describe how evaluation differs from the behavior-data distribution and whether the policy is constrained or regularized near dataset support.
entries.meaning: Good performance on held-out samples drawn from familiar coverage does not by itself establish reliable action selection in unsupported regions.

provenance.note: Independent scope guidance based on offline-RL distribution-shift analyses.

entries.avoid: Do not call a full model-generated episode or an arbitrary imagined trajectory a branched rollout without specifying the real-data branch point.
examples: We start $k$-step model rollouts from states in the replay buffer and add the synthetic transitions to {training buffer}.
Each branched rollout follows the current policy for {length} learned transitions.
entries.guidance: Report the branch-state distribution, rollout length, policy used inside the model, and how synthetic and real transitions enter learning.
entries.meaning: A finite learned-model rollout initialized from a state sampled from real experience, used to generate synthetic transitions without simulating an entire episode from the initial-state distribution.

provenance.note: Independent definition of the branched-rollout construction introduced and analyzed in MBPO.

entries.avoid: Do not infer physical consistency, controllability, or policy utility solely from visually plausible generated video.
examples: We use an embodied world model to predict {future sensory or geometric state} conditioned on {robot action sequence}.
The model supports {planning or policy learning} by coupling {environment prediction} with {action representation}.
entries.guidance: Specify the predicted modalities and geometry, action conditioning, temporal horizon, and downstream decision use. Contemporary methods differ substantially, so treat this as an umbrella term rather than a fixed architecture.
entries.meaning: An action-aware predictive model of how an embodied environment evolves in space and time, designed to support capabilities such as planning, policy learning, or interaction prediction.

provenance.note: Independent synthesis of linked primary sources; no source sentence copied.

entries.avoid: Do not interchange inverse dynamics with model inversion unless the mapping and objective are actually equivalent.
examples: The forward model predicts {next state} from {state and action}, while the inverse model predicts {action} from {state pair or goal}.
Joint training couples action prediction with {video or latent dynamics prediction}.
entries.guidance: Define the conditioning variables precisely; inverse dynamics may be ambiguous when multiple actions can produce similar transitions.
entries.meaning: Forward dynamics predicts a future state or observation from a current state and action, whereas inverse dynamics infers an action from a state transition or desired outcome.

provenance.note: Independent synthesis of linked primary sources; no source sentence copied.

entries.avoid: Do not call an arbitrary feature vector a state without explaining its temporal role.
examples: The latent state summarizes {observation history} for predicting {future quantity}.
We infer {latent state} from {observation and previous state}.
entries.guidance: Explain whether the state is Markovian by assumption or approximation, how it is inferred, and which downstream quantities depend on it. State separately when task objectives make the representation task-oriented.
entries.meaning: A learned representation intended to retain information relevant to the modeled or predicted quantities while abstracting away some details of raw observations.

provenance.note: Independent synthesis of linked primary sources; no source sentence copied.

entries.avoid: Do not conflate model-based RL with supervised next-step prediction that never affects decisions.
examples: The method is model-based because the learned dynamics model is used to {plan actions or optimize the policy}.
Model-based reinforcement learning can use predicted transitions for {downstream decision process}.
entries.guidance: Explain the role of the model rather than applying the label solely because the architecture contains a predictor.
entries.meaning: Reinforcement learning that uses a model of environment dynamics, learned or known, to improve decision making through planning, synthetic experience, value estimation, or policy optimization.

provenance.note: Independent synthesis of linked primary sources; no source sentence copied.

entries.avoid: Do not assume that any predicted variance is calibrated or that it cleanly separates aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty.
examples: We learn a probabilistic dynamics model $p_\theta(s_{t+1}\mid s_t,a_t)$ and propagate multiple particles during planning.
The latent transition predicts a distribution over {next latent variable} conditioned on {state and action}.
entries.guidance: State what is random, how the distribution is parameterized, and whether it is intended to model environment stochasticity, model uncertainty, or both.
entries.meaning: A dynamics model that represents a conditional distribution over future states or latent states rather than returning only one point prediction.

provenance.note: Independent synthesis of probabilistic dynamics formulations in the listed primary papers.

entries.avoid: Do not treat 'task-oriented' and 'implicit' as general synonyms, or claim that reconstruction is unnecessary for every task family.
examples: We learn a task-oriented latent dynamics model using {reward, value, and consistency objectives} rather than pixel reconstruction.
The model predicts {decision-relevant quantities} in latent space.
entries.guidance: Name the task signals, such as reward, value, or latent consistency, that shape the representation. Use 'implicit world model' only when a cited paper defines that label for its own model.
entries.meaning: A latent dynamics model trained to preserve decision-relevant predictive structure without necessarily reconstructing raw observations.

provenance.note: Independent synthesis of linked primary sources; no source sentence copied.

entries.avoid: Do not imply safety or robustness solely because the planner propagates a distribution.
examples: The planner samples predictive dynamics and optimizes expected return under the resulting trajectory distribution.
We penalize candidate plans with high {validated uncertainty statistic}.
entries.guidance: State whether uncertainty is marginalized, sampled, penalized, or used as a constraint. Distinguish predictive uncertainty from risk preference.
entries.meaning: Planning that represents or uses uncertainty in learned dynamics when evaluating candidate action sequences, rather than optimizing only a single deterministic forecast.

provenance.note: Independent definition synthesized from uncertainty-aware model-based planning formulations.

entries.avoid: Do not infer physical consistency or control utility from visual realism alone.
examples: The visual world model predicts {RGB, depth, or semantics} at {future viewpoints} conditioned on {agent path or actions}.
We evaluate whether predicted observations support {navigation or manipulation decision}.
entries.expression: visual world model for embodied agents
entries.guidance: Specify predicted modalities, spatial frame, action or path conditioning, and whether the output is used by the agent. Separate plausible generation from geometrically accurate prediction.
entries.meaning: A predictive model that represents how an embodied agent's visual environment may evolve, often conditioned on motion or actions and used for navigation, planning, or policy learning.

provenance.note: Independent synthesis of linked primary sources; no source sentence copied.

entries.avoid: Do not treat every video generator or static scene representation as a world model without an action, temporal, or decision-making connection.
examples: We use a world model to predict {future latent states or observations} conditioned on {current state and action sequence}.
Here, world model refers to {learned transition components} used for {planning or policy optimization}.
entries.guidance: State what variables the model predicts, whether prediction occurs in observation or latent space, and how the model is used downstream. Community usage is broad, so define the paper's operational scope.
entries.meaning: A learned predictive model of how an environment evolves, typically conditioned on the agent's actions and used to support prediction, planning, or policy learning.

provenance.note: Independent synthesis of linked primary sources; no source sentence copied.

entries.avoid: Do not force methods into mutually exclusive categories when they combine mechanisms.
examples: World-model methods can be organized by the space in which they predict, the objectives used to learn the representation, and whether decisions arise from online planning or policy learning in imagination.
entries.expression: World-model methods can be organized by {representation}, {training objective}, and {decision mechanism}.
entries.guidance: Instantiate each axis with verified method families: observation-space versus latent prediction, reconstruction versus task-oriented objectives, and online planning versus imagined policy learning.
entries.meaning: Provides a technical-axis structure for a world-model related-work paragraph.

provenance.note: Independent synthesis of linked primary sources; example wording is original.

entries.avoid: Do not infer controllability from temporal prediction alone or relabel viewpoint conditioning as action conditioning.
examples: The model learns action-conditioned dynamics over {latent state or sensory representation}.
Conditioning on actions allows the model to evaluate {candidate action sequences}.
entries.guidance: Use to distinguish controllable prediction from passive video prediction. Specify action representation, temporal alignment, and prediction target. Use 'path-conditioned' or 'viewpoint-conditioned' when a model conditions on a planned path rather than low-level actions.
entries.meaning: Predictive dynamics in which future states or observations depend explicitly on the agent's action sequence.

provenance.note: Canonical term indexed from linked primary papers; examples are original.

entries.avoid: Do not write 'errors exponentially explode' without a bound or measurement supporting that rate.
examples: Long model rollouts are susceptible to compounding model error as predictions feed into subsequent transitions.
We limit the rollout horizon to {H} to reduce error accumulation.
entries.guidance: Tie the claim to rollout horizon, distribution shift, and the evaluated quantity. Distinguish accumulation from a formally exponential error rate unless proven.
entries.meaning: Prediction errors that accumulate as a learned model is recursively unrolled, potentially moving rollouts away from states represented in the training data.

provenance.note: Canonical term indexed from linked primary papers; examples are original.

entries.avoid: Do not equate discreteness with symbolic or interpretable representation.
examples: The world model encodes observations into a discrete latent representation parameterized by {categorical structure}.
entries.guidance: Describe the parameterization and estimator used for learning. Attribute benefits such as optimization stability or expressivity only to verified experiments.
entries.meaning: A latent representation whose stochastic variables take values from discrete categories rather than a continuous distribution.

provenance.note: Canonical term indexed from linked primary papers; examples are original.

entries.avoid: Do not present an ensemble as an exact Bayesian posterior or treat members trained identically as independent evidence.
examples: We fit an ensemble of {number} dynamics models and sample a member when propagating each particle.
Planning penalizes action sequences with high ensemble disagreement.
entries.guidance: Describe initialization, data resampling, ensemble size, and how predictions are combined or sampled. Call disagreement a heuristic for epistemic uncertainty unless a stronger interpretation is justified.
entries.meaning: A collection of separately fitted dynamics predictors whose aggregate predictions can improve robustness and provide a practical disagreement signal.

provenance.note: Field-standard terminology indexed from uncertainty-aware model-based RL papers.

entries.avoid: Do not call logged or simulator-generated trajectories imagined merely because they are off-policy.
examples: We generate imagined trajectories of length {H} from latent states inferred from the replay buffer.
Model rollouts provide {training targets} for {policy or value function}.
entries.guidance: Use 'imagined trajectories' for Dreamer-style latent rollouts and 'model rollouts' as the broader term. Report rollout horizon and starting-state distribution.
entries.meaning: Sequences of predicted states, rewards, or observations generated by repeatedly applying a learned model under a chosen action sequence or policy.

provenance.note: Canonical term indexed from linked primary papers; examples are original.

entries.avoid: Do not imply that operating in latent space automatically yields accurate long-horizon predictions.
examples: We learn a latent dynamics model that maps {latent state, action} to {next latent state distribution}.
Planning is performed by unrolling the latent dynamics model over {horizon} steps.
entries.guidance: Specify the latent state, deterministic and stochastic components if relevant, and the training signals that make it useful for the downstream task.
entries.meaning: A transition model that predicts the evolution of a learned latent state rather than directly predicting raw observations.

provenance.note: Canonical term indexed from linked primary papers; examples are original.

entries.avoid: Do not anthropomorphize the model or imply physical execution.
examples: The actor and critic are optimized on trajectories generated through latent imagination.
Latent imagination enables {policy update} without additional environment interaction.
entries.guidance: Use for model-generated trajectories rather than replayed environment trajectories. State how imagined data trains or evaluates the policy/value function.
entries.meaning: The generation of hypothetical future state sequences by unrolling a learned dynamics model in latent space.

provenance.note: Canonical term indexed from linked primary papers; examples are original.

entries.avoid: Do not use 'dynamic model' when referring to environment dynamics; that phrase can mean a model that changes over time.
examples: The learned dynamics model predicts {next representation} from {current representation} and {action}.
entries.guidance: Use 'dynamics model' for the transition component; use 'world model' when the broader system may also include representation, observation, reward, continuation, or uncertainty components.
entries.meaning: A model fitted from data to predict state or latent-state transitions under actions.

provenance.note: Canonical term indexed from linked primary papers; examples are original.

entries.avoid: Do not conflate a learned reward predictor with human preference modeling or with the complete world model.
examples: The latent model jointly predicts rewards and observations from the recurrent state.
Planning evaluates imagined trajectories with a learned reward predictor $r_\theta(z_t,a_t)$.
entries.guidance: Specify its inputs, target, loss, and whether the environment reward function is otherwise available at planning time.
entries.meaning: A component that predicts task reward from modeled states, latent states, actions, or transitions when reward is included in the learned world-model objective.

provenance.note: Field-standard component terminology indexed from latent world-model methods.

entries.avoid: Do not equate low average one-step validation loss with negligible policy-relevant model bias.
examples: Long synthetic rollouts can amplify model bias when the policy visits state–action pairs poorly covered by real data.
We evaluate model error under the current policy distribution rather than only on the training split.
entries.expression: model bias in model-based reinforcement learning
entries.guidance: Identify the state–action distribution and downstream quantity affected. Separate model bias from finite-sample variance and generic policy-estimation error.
entries.meaning: Distortion in policy learning or planning caused by systematic discrepancies between learned model transitions and the environment transitions relevant to the evaluated policy.

provenance.note: Field-standard term indexed from analyses of learned-model usage in policy optimization.

entries.avoid: Do not label every performance gap as model exploitation without showing that optimization interacts with model error.
examples: The policy may exploit optimistic model errors outside the support of the collected transitions.
Constraining planning to {supported region} reduces opportunities for model exploitation.
entries.guidance: Use the term when the optimizer or policy actively seeks regions where model errors are favorable. Support the diagnosis with real-environment evaluation or an appropriate uncertainty/error analysis.
entries.meaning: A failure mode in which optimization selects actions that look favorable under an inaccurate learned model but do not yield the predicted outcomes in the real environment.

provenance.note: Field-standard failure-mode terminology synthesized from model-based RL analyses.

entries.avoid: Do not use MPC as a synonym for any policy that consumes model predictions.
examples: At each environment step, MPC optimizes {candidate action sequences} over a horizon of {H} and executes {first action or action chunk}.
We augment the finite-horizon objective with {terminal value estimate}.
entries.guidance: State the planning horizon, optimizer, objective, terminal value, and how many actions are executed before replanning.
entries.meaning: A control strategy that repeatedly optimizes a finite-horizon action sequence using a model, executes an initial portion, and replans from the new state.

provenance.note: Canonical term indexed from linked primary papers; examples are original.

entries.avoid: Do not refer to a transition model as a decoder.
examples: An observation model decodes the latent state into {pixels, depth, or other sensory prediction}.
Our task-oriented model omits an observation decoder and is trained with {predictive objective}.
entries.guidance: Use 'decoder' when emphasizing architecture and 'observation model' when emphasizing the probabilistic generative role. Some task-oriented world models intentionally omit it.
entries.meaning: A component that maps a latent state to a distribution over observations or reconstructs observation-space outputs.

provenance.note: Canonical term indexed from linked primary papers; examples are original.

entries.avoid: Do not call a single open-loop plan receding-horizon control.
examples: We use receding-horizon planning to reoptimize the action sequence every {k} steps.
entries.guidance: Use when replanning closes the loop. Distinguish action horizon from prediction horizon and note whether an action chunk rather than one action is executed.
entries.meaning: Planning in which a finite-horizon solution is repeatedly recomputed as new observations become available.

provenance.note: Canonical term indexed from linked primary papers; examples are original.

entries.avoid: Do not claim that stochastic latents capture calibrated uncertainty unless calibration is evaluated.
examples: The model samples a stochastic latent state from {posterior or prior distribution} at each step.
entries.guidance: Distinguish stochasticity in the latent transition from randomness in policy actions or observation noise. Name the distributional parameterization when relevant.
entries.meaning: A latent state represented by a distribution or sampled variable to capture uncertainty or multiple possible futures.

provenance.note: Canonical term indexed from linked primary papers; examples are original.

entries.avoid: Do not use the term as a synonym for collecting real environment trajectories or for generic Monte Carlo evaluation without a learned model.
examples: We propagate {number} particles through the probabilistic ensemble and rank candidate action sequences by their predicted returns.
Each particle samples {model or transition noise} according to {sampling rule}.
entries.guidance: Specify the particle count, how ensemble members are selected across time, and how predicted returns are aggregated for action selection.
entries.meaning: A sampling procedure that propagates multiple hypothetical trajectories through a probabilistic dynamics model to approximate distributions over future outcomes.

provenance.note: Method terminology indexed from PETS and paraphrased for reusable technical writing.

entries.avoid: Do not claim perfect decomposition merely because a network predicts a variance and an ensemble produces disagreement.
examples: The output distribution represents conditional stochasticity, while ensemble disagreement serves as a practical proxy for model uncertainty.
We do not assume that the two uncertainty sources are perfectly identifiable from the available transitions.
entries.expression: aleatoric versus epistemic uncertainty in learned dynamics
entries.guidance: Explain which modeling component is intended to represent each uncertainty and validate the interpretation when it matters to planning or risk.
entries.meaning: Aleatoric uncertainty describes conditional variability that remains even with complete knowledge, whereas epistemic uncertainty reflects limited knowledge about the predictive model and may shrink with informative data.

provenance.note: Independent scope guidance based on the uncertainty treatment in PETS.

entries.avoid: Do not use low one-step loss as the sole evidence that a model supports long-horizon planning.
examples: Although the model achieves low one-step error, we separately evaluate rollout fidelity over {horizon}.
One-step prediction accuracy does not by itself establish decision-relevant long-horizon fidelity.
entries.expression: one-step accuracy does not by itself establish long-horizon fidelity
entries.guidance: Report multi-step or task-level metrics when the downstream method unrolls the model. Specify open-loop versus closed-loop evaluation.
entries.meaning: Accurate next-step prediction and stable recursive rollout are related but distinct evaluation properties.

provenance.note: Independent synthesis of linked primary sources; no source sentence copied.

entries.avoid: Do not classify all world-model methods as planners.
examples: Whereas {method family} performs online planning in the learned model, {method family} trains a policy on imagined trajectories.
Our method combines {online trajectory optimization} with {learned value or policy prior}.
entries.expression: online planning versus policy learning in imagination
entries.guidance: State when computation occurs and whether the deployed controller replans. This is a useful axis for organizing related work.
entries.meaning: World models may support decisions by optimizing actions at test time, by training an amortized policy on imagined experience, or by combining both.

provenance.note: Independent synthesis of linked primary sources; no source sentence copied.

entries.avoid: Do not state that shorter or longer model rollouts are universally better across data regimes and tasks.
examples: We use a rollout horizon of {k}; longer rollouts degrade {metric} as prediction errors accumulate.
The rollout horizon increases from {a} to {b} as the model is trained on more real data.
entries.expression: model rollout horizon trades synthetic coverage against accumulated error
entries.guidance: Treat rollout length as an algorithmic choice tied to model accuracy and policy shift. Report its schedule and include a sensitivity study when central to the claim.
entries.meaning: Increasing the number of learned transitions can provide more synthetic experience but also exposes training or planning to errors that compound under the rollout distribution.

provenance.note: Independent usage guidance based on short-rollout model-based RL and latent planning work.
